strengths: AutoSeg addresses a practical limitation of open-vocabulary segmentation: requiring users to supply relevant categories. BBoost’s use of clustered BLIP patch embeddings for local caption generation is an interesting technical contribution that requires no additional weight training.

The experiments provide meaningful evidence for improved vocabulary generation. With the same X-Decoder segmentor, Table 1 improves class-agnostic mIoU over plain BLIP captions across all four datasets, including 38.0 to 71.8 on VOC. Table 3 also shows a substantial VOC improvement over LLaVA plus X-Decoder, from 56.7 to 87.1 mIoU.

LAVE addresses a real evaluation difficulty involving synonyms and semantic hierarchies. Its results differ from manual mapping by only 0.2–1.1 mIoU across the four datasets, providing useful preliminary validation.

The overall pipeline is understandable, the principal models and datasets are credited, and implementation parameters and evaluator pseudocode are supplied. The qualitative examples illustrate capabilities beyond fixed dataset labels, while the supplementary failure cases candidly expose hallucinations and vocabulary competition.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol remains insufficiently validated. Section 9.3 relies on the LLM’s knowledge of the PC/ADE vocabularies rather than supplying their class lists, and instructs it to map stuff terms to background despite these benchmarks containing stuff classes. Algorithm 1’s exact-name override does not resolve non-exact synonyms. Furthermore, it is unclear whether ZeroSeg was reevaluated using the same mapper. This matters because Table A7 shows a 13.2-point VOC difference from changing only the mapper. Aggregate agreement with manual mapping is encouraging but does not establish mapping accuracy or comparison fairness.

The separation between model selection and evaluation is unclear. Section 5.1 reports Bayesian optimization on VOC annotations without identifying a disjoint tuning split. Tables 2–4 appear to use the best caption-cycle count for each evaluation dataset. The annotation-free framing should acknowledge this supervision, and results should use a clearly separated selection protocol. Repeated-run variability is also missing despite stochastic captioning; this is particularly relevant to the small PC advantage of 11.7 versus 11.4 mIoU.

The central claim of more precise, comprehensive open-ended recognition is supported mainly by selected examples and vocabulary counts. Producing more unique nouns does not establish their correctness or image-specific coverage. Mapping predictions back to coarse benchmark classes can conceal incorrect fine-grained labels. A systematic audit of generated category precision, coverage, and corresponding masks would strengthen this contribution.

Important details of BBoost are ambiguous. Equation 9 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments, which are not equivalent to the stated Hungarian matching. The alignment of 24×24 and 32×32 patch grids is unspecified, as is how the concatenated 256-dimensional positional features are handled before entering the frozen BLIP decoder. These affect reproduction of the proposed mechanism.

Evidence for broader applicability and efficiency is limited. BBoost is evaluated with only X-Decoder, and the contributions of multiple resolutions and cross-clustering alignment are not isolated. No runtime or memory measurements substantiate efficiency claims for a pipeline using 14 clustering runs and up to 25 captioning cycles.

A reporting inconsistency needs correction: Table A6 specifies one captioning cycle but reports 87.1 VOC mIoU, whereas Table 2 reports 85.3 for one cycle and 87.1 for ten. This may be a correctable presentation error, but the configuration must be reconciled to interpret the denoising ablation.
